headline: How Claude Code's Creator Actually Writes Software
lede: Boris Cherny, the Head of Claude Code at Anthropic, published his personal development workflow in January 2026 — and it is more methodical than the hype suggests. He runs roughly fifteen concurrent Claude instances across terminal and browser, uses the largest available model, and ships twenty to thirty pull requests a day.
body:
**Boris Cherny** built what would become one of the most-used AI coding tools on the planet as a side project during his first month at Anthropic. A former principal engineer at Meta (META) who briefly detoured through the AI code-editor startup Cursor, Cherny released Claude Code publicly in May 2025; the tool now accounts for roughly 4% of all public GitHub commits, with daily active users doubling month-over-month at its peak.

At any given moment Cherny manages fifteen concurrent Claude sessions. Five live in numbered iTerm2 tabs, each pointed at a separate full *git checkout* of the same repository — not a branch, not a *worktree*, but a distinct on-disk clone — so parallel agents never collide on file locks or shared state. Another five to ten sessions run on claude.ai/code simultaneously; he starts them from his iOS app in the morning and resumes on his laptop later, with desktop notifications alerting him when any tab needs attention.

For the model, he uses **Claude Opus 4.5 with extended thinking** exclusively and argues it is paradoxically faster than lighter alternatives. The reasoning: it requires less steering and makes fewer tool-use errors, finishing tasks in fewer total round-trips. Every task begins in *Plan Mode* (Shift+Tab twice in the terminal), where Cherny iterates on a plan before allowing execution. Only once the plan satisfies him does he flip to auto-accept edits and let the model one-shot the implementation. The result is twenty to thirty merged pull requests per day.

Two infrastructure choices underpin that velocity. Each team's repository carries a *CLAUDE.md* file — roughly 2,500 tokens of accumulated institutional knowledge: style conventions, design guidelines, known failure modes, PR templates. Cherny tags colleagues' pull-request reviews with @claude so the model can propose updates to CLAUDE.md as lessons accumulate. He also connects Claude Code to a suite of *MCP servers* (Model Context Protocol plug-ins that give the agent live access to external systems): Slack for messaging, BigQuery for analytics, Sentry for error logs, and a Chrome extension for visual verification. A *PostToolUse hook* fires an auto-formatter after every file edit.

The bookmark's framing as a guide to “vibecoding” — Andrej Karpathy's February 2025 coinage for fully AI-delegated programming, where the developer steers by intuition and the model writes every line — is slightly imprecise. Cherny's workflow is something stricter: mandatory planning phases, systematic parallelism, and institutional-memory tooling built to outlast any single session. It lives within the same broad shift away from line-by-line authorship, but the discipline distinguishes it from the casual interpretation that earned *vibe coding* Collins English Dictionary's Word of the Year for 2025.

concepts.definition: A term coined by Andrej Karpathy in February 2025 for a style of programming where the developer describes intent in natural language and fully delegates code-writing to an AI model. The programmer steers, tests, and gives feedback rather than typing code manually. Collins English Dictionary named it Word of the Year for 2025.

A Claude Code feature (activated with Shift+Tab twice) that puts the AI into a read-only planning state before it makes any file edits. The developer and model iterate on an approach until the plan is satisfactory, then execution is enabled. It reduces wasted work caused by early incorrect assumptions.

A Claude model feature that allocates extra internal computation time for the model to reason step by step before responding. It trades speed for output quality, and is most useful on complex, multi-step coding or analytical tasks.

Model Context Protocol servers: plug-ins that give an AI coding agent structured, authorised access to external tools and data sources such as databases, error-monitoring services, or messaging platforms. First published as an open standard by Anthropic in late 2024.

A markdown file placed in a git repository that Claude Code reads automatically on startup. Teams use it to encode institutional knowledge — coding conventions, architectural decisions, known pitfalls — so the model behaves consistently without needing to be re-prompted each session.

A Git feature that lets you check out multiple branches of the same repository into different directories simultaneously, sharing a single .git folder. Cherny goes further by using fully separate repository clones, giving each Claude instance a completely independent on-disk state.

A Claude Code mode in which file changes proposed by the model are applied automatically without requiring manual confirmation for each edit. It is typically enabled after a plan has been reviewed, allowing the model to implement an entire task in a single uninterrupted pass.

A Claude Code automation hook that fires a shell command immediately after the model uses a tool such as writing a file. Cherny uses it to run an auto-formatter so that every AI-generated code edit is consistently formatted before he reviews it.

books.title: Programming TypeScript
books.author: Boris Cherny
books.summary: An O'Reilly title by Cherny that teaches TypeScript from first principles, covering the type system, generics, and advanced patterns for building safe, maintainable JavaScript applications. It is widely used in corporate engineering onboarding. Its existence signals that Cherny was a respected practitioner-author well before moving into AI tooling.

fact_check: The bookmark states Cherny “runs another 10 sessions” beyond his five terminal tabs — the primary source describes five to ten additional sessions on claude.ai/code, so ten is the upper bound, not a fixed figure. The total of roughly fifteen concurrent instances is accurate. The “creator” framing is slightly loose: Cherny built the original version as a side project in his first month at Anthropic and is now Head of Claude Code, but the tool has grown with a full team behind it.
